email_subject: Urgent: Q2 Budget Reallocation Approval Needed
email_body: Hi, I need you to urgently transfer $250,000 to our new vendor account before the end of the day. The details are attached in the invoice. Please confirm once done.
indicators: The email appears to come from the CEO but the sending domain is a close spoof of the official domain (companydomain.co instead of companydomain.com); The request is urgent and involves a large financial transfer, creating pressure to bypass normal verification; The attachment contains a fake invoice with altered bank details; The language is slightly off from usual executive communication style; There is no prior discussion or official approval trail for this transaction

email_subject: Confidential: Updated Passwords for Project Apollo
email_body: Please urgently provide the new credentials for the Project Apollo server. Our system audit flagged multiple access issues. Send them back encrypted as soon as possible.
indicators: Sender email is spoofed to appear as CTO but originates from an external IP address; Unusual request asking to disclose sensitive credentials via email; Use of urgency and confidentiality to pressure the recipient; No prior security audit was communicated to the engineering team; No secure channel is requested for sharing credentials

email_subject: Meeting Follow-up: Please Review and Approve Wire Transfer
email_body: Following up on our discussion, please approve the attached wire transfer of $500,000 to our partner company. The payment is critical for the ongoing project delivery.
indicators: Email sender address is a lookalike domain (finance.manager@company-domain.com); Attachment contains macro-enabled document that can execute malicious code; The request bypasses the established multi-step financial verification process; The wire transfer details differ from standard vendor payment accounts; Urgency and pressure tactics to prevent the recipient from verifying
